extracted.intended_audience: Putnam contestants, graders, coaches, and competitive undergraduate undergraduate mathematicians
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and scoring rules used to evaluate individual Putnam Competition problem solutions and to guide how contestants should write solutions to receive full credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring scale (per problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of 12 problems is worth 10 points. Possible scores per problem: 0, 1, 2, 8, 9, 10. The scores 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 are essentially never awarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the discrete set of allowable per-problem scores; graders should map a solution to one of these values rather than interpolate. Used to implement the Putnam's distinctive partial-credit scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gap of Death (3–7)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Only virtually perfect solutions receive 8 or more points; flawed solutions fall below the 'Gap of Death' between 3 and 7 points."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Putnam graders intentionally enforce a binary judgment: either the solution is correct (with at most cosmetic flaws), or it is not. There is no credit for 'I had the right idea'. The gap discourages awarding middling partial credit for plausible-sounding but incomplete/wrong arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score 10 (meaning)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solution must be essentially flawless: full proof of every step, all cases handled, clear presentation. This is the target for a 'good' Putnam solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score 9 (meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: 9 — Correct argument, one minor slip (algebra typo, missed degenerate case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when the main argument is correct but there is a minor, easily explainable error or omission that does not undermine the central reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score 8 (meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: 8 — Correct main argument; small but nontrivial gap easily filled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awarded when the core method and argument are correct but a nontrivial detail is omitted that a reader/grader can fill quickly; still near-perfect in substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score 2 (meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: 2 — Some genuine progress beyond restating the problem; key insight missing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes partial, meaningful work that indicates understanding of some structure of the problem but lacks the crucial idea to complete a solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score 1 (meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 — A correct but trivial observation; nothing substantive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given for tiny, elementary observations that do not materially advance toward a solution beyond restatement or trivial manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score 0 (meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: 0 — No progress; or argument contains a fatal flaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigned where the submission gives no meaningful advance or includes reasoning that is fundamentally incorrect or impossible to repair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Putnam philosophy: problem either solved or not
rubrics_metrics.description: The Putnam philosophy: a math problem is either solved or not. Awarding 5 points for 'I almost had it' rewards plausible-sounding but wrong arguments. The Gap forces graders to make a binary judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides overall grading attitude: prefer strong evidentiary proof over awarding reward for incomplete heuristics or promising attempts. Explains rationale for discrete scoring set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good solution must be a 10
rubrics_metrics.description: "A solution is good only if it would receive a 10."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets contestant expectations: to be considered a proper solution in Putnam standards, the write-up must meet the full criteria for 10 points (correct, complete, well-presented). This sentence motivates the subsequent forced behaviors for writing solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every step proved
rubrics_metrics.description: Every step proved — no 'clearly', no 'easy to see'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not skip justification by relying on reader inference. Even elementary steps should be written/argued if they are needed for correctness; avoid hand-waving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every case handled
rubrics_metrics.description: Every case handled — no missed degenerate case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly consider and resolve all cases and special/degenerate scenarios the problem or argument creates; omission of cases can be fatal to receiving high credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every quantifier explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Every quantifier explicit — no implicit 'for all sufficiently large'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make universal/existential quantifiers and ranges clear; avoid informal phrases that hide domain or scope, which can conceal gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify any claimed witness
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification of any claimed witness — if you say 'consider x = 7', show 7 works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever a specific example, witness, or construction is asserted to satisfy conditions, include a verification rather than assuming it is obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest treatment of what's missing
rubrics_metrics.description: Honest treatment of what's missing — if a step is hard, prove it; don't paper over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a sub-claim or lemma is nontrivial, provide a proof or clearly indicate why it follows; do not assert difficult facts without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legibility
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write clearly and organize the solution so graders can follow reasoning without effort; poor handwriting or disorganized presentation can cost points independent of mathematical correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion stated
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusion stated — the final answer in a box, with the actual question's wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the final answer and connect it to the problem's requirement; clearly mark the end of the solution so graders can verify that the asked claim was proved.
